lesson_title: Two Taxi Routes, One Lying Average
hook_text: Both posters say 'average trip: 30 minutes'. One route will make you late. The average will never tell you which.
clip_script: Two taxi routes both claim the same thing on their poster: average trip to town, 30 minutes. Route one: trips take 28, 29, 30, 31 or 32 minutes. Route two: trips take 15, 20, 30, 40 or 45 minutes. Both average exactly 30 — yet you would never call them the same service. On route one you can promise your boss an arrival time. On route two you might be early, or you might be very late, and the average printed on the poster hides that completely. The number that exposes the difference is spread: route one's times wander 4 minutes end to end; route two's wander 30. Same centre, wildly different reliability — and that is why statisticians never report an average alone. Centre tells you where the middle is. Spread tells you whether to trust it.
visual_style: Split screen of two minibus taxis racing timeline bars: route one's five trip-time markers clustered tight around 30, route two's scattered wide, then a measuring tape snapping across each cluster showing 4 versus 30.
pacing: Quick poster reveal, rhythmic listing of trip times, dramatic pause on 'same average', decisive finish on the two ranges.
